consensus_summary: Worship is reverent homage, adoration, and self-surrender directed to God alone, expressed through bowing, praise, service, obedience, liturgy, and whole-life devotion.
book_summary: Worship is bodily bowing joined to obedient service and allegiance to God, visibly expressing fear of the LORD according to his appointed terms; singing or the “song service” is classified separately as praise rather than worship itself.
consensus_core_identification: Reverent homage and submissive devotion to God alone.
book_core_identification: Bodily homage and lived allegiance or service to God alone.
boundary_disagreement: The book restricts worship more tightly to bowing or embodied homage together with service and covenantal allegiance. It excludes or reclassifies singing by itself—and especially the church song segment commonly called “worship”—as praise rather than worship, whereas the consensus commonly includes praise and singing among worship’s expressions.
material_contradiction: There is no replacement of the consensus’s central referent: both identify worship with homage and submission to God. The material disagreement concerns whether praise and singing count as worship themselves and whether visible bodily homage and divinely appointed conditions are defining requirements.
rationale: The book retains the consensus core of exclusive homage and submission to God but gives it a more concrete and restrictive boundary: bowing in the body and serving in life. Its denial that the song service is worship materially reclassifies cases that broad Christian usage often includes, making the entry refined rather than fully matching or divergent.
strongest_objection: The cited texts strongly associate worship with bowing, fear, and service, and 2 Chronicles 20:18–19 distinguishes falling in worship from subsequently standing to praise. However, these passages alone do not establish that bodily bowing is always necessary, that worship must occur only at appointed times, or that singing can never itself function as worship; the narrative distinction in one scene may not define a universal lexical boundary.
